questions.title: Atomic radius of palladium from its density
questions.body_md: Calculate the radius of a palladium atom, given that Pd has an FCC crystal structure, a density of $12.0\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ and an atomic weight of $106.4\ \mathrm{g/mol}$.
questions.solution_md:
### What is given

- Pd, FCC crystal structure
- Density $\rho = 12.0\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$
- Atomic mass $A_{\mathrm{Pd}} = 106.4\ \mathrm{g/mol}$

### Set up the density relation

For FCC there are $n = 4$ atoms per unit cell, the cube edge is $a = 2R\sqrt{2}$, and so the cell volume is $V_C = a^3 = 16R^3\sqrt{2}$. The density of a crystal is

$$\rho = \frac{nA}{V_C N_A}$$

where $n$ is the number of atoms per unit cell, $A$ the atomic mass, $V_C$ the unit cell volume and $N_A$ Avogadro's number.

### Substitute

$$\rho_{\mathrm{Pd}} = \frac{4\,(106.4\ \mathrm{g/mol})}{\left(16R^3\sqrt{2}\right)\left(6.023\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{atoms/mol}\right)} = 12.0\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

### Solve for $R$

$$R = \sqrt[3]{\frac{4\,(106.4)}{\left(16\sqrt{2}\right)\left(12.0\right)\left(6.023\times10^{23}\right)}} = 1.38\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.138\ \mathrm{nm}$$

questions.title: Is niobium FCC or BCC?
questions.body_md: Niobium has an atomic radius of $0.1430\ \mathrm{nm}$ and a density of $8.57\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Determine whether it has an FCC or a BCC crystal structure.
questions.solution_md:
### What is known

- $A_{\mathrm{Nb}} = 92.91\ \mathrm{g/mol}$
- $R = 0.1430\ \mathrm{nm} = 1.43\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$
- Density $\rho = 8.57\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$

The method is to compute the density each structure would give and see which one matches, using

$$\rho = \frac{nA}{a^3 N_A}$$

### Test FCC

If Nb were FCC then $n = 4$ and $a = 2R\sqrt{2}$:

$$\rho = \frac{nA}{\left(2R\sqrt{2}\right)^3 N_A} = \frac{4\times92.91}{\left(2\times1.43\times10^{-8}\sqrt{2}\right)^3\times6.023\times10^{23}} = 9.33\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

That is not the measured value.

### Test BCC

If Nb were BCC then $n = 2$ and $a = \dfrac{4R}{\sqrt{3}}$:

$$\rho = \frac{nA}{\left(\frac{4R}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3 N_A} = \frac{2\times92.91}{\left(\frac{4\times1.43\times10^{-8}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3\times6.023\times10^{23}} = 8.57\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

This matches the density given in the problem statement, so niobium has a BCC crystal structure.

questions.title: Volume change when iron transforms from BCC to FCC
questions.body_md: What is the fractional volume change in iron as it transforms from BCC to FCC at $910\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Assume that the lattice parameter $a$ is $0.2910\ \mathrm{nm}$ for BCC iron and $0.3647\ \mathrm{nm}$ for FCC iron.
questions.solution_md:
### The quantity to compare

The two structures pack different numbers of atoms into a cell, so the cells themselves are not comparable. What is comparable is the volume *per atom*: the unit cell volume divided by the number of atoms it contains.

### BCC iron

There are 2 atoms per unit cell in the BCC structure, so

$$V_{\mathrm{BCC}} = \frac{a^3}{2} = \frac{(0.2910\ \mathrm{nm})^3}{2} = 0.01232\ \mathrm{nm^3/atom}$$

### FCC iron

There are 4 atoms per unit cell in the FCC structure, so

$$V_{\mathrm{FCC}} = \frac{a^3}{4} = \frac{(0.3647\ \mathrm{nm})^3}{4} = 0.01213\ \mathrm{nm^3/atom}$$

### Fractional change

$$\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{FCC}} - V_{\mathrm{BCC}}}{V_{\mathrm{BCC}}} = \frac{0.01213 - 0.01232}{0.01232} = -0.0157$$

There is a $1.57\%$ contraction. Iron gets denser on becoming FCC, which is what you would expect: FCC is a close-packed structure and BCC is not.

questions.title: Atomic radius of tantalum from its density
questions.body_md: Calculate the radius of a tantalum atom, given that it has a BCC crystal structure, a density of $16.6\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ and an atomic weight of $180.9\ \mathrm{g/mol}$.
questions.solution_md:
### Set up the BCC cell volume

For BCC there are $n = 2$ atoms per unit cell and the cube edge is $a = \dfrac{4R}{\sqrt{3}}$, so

$$V_C = a^3 = \left(\frac{4R}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3 = \frac{64R^3}{3\sqrt{3}}$$

### Substitute into the density relation

$$\rho = \frac{nA}{V_C N_A} = \frac{2 A_{\mathrm{Ta}}}{\left(\frac{64R^3}{3\sqrt{3}}\right) N_A}$$

### Solve for $R$

$$R = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3\sqrt{3}\,(2)(180.9)}{64\,(16.6)\left(6.023\times10^{23}\right)}} = 1.43\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.143\ \mathrm{nm}$$

questions.title: Is rhodium FCC or BCC?
questions.body_md: Rhodium has an atomic radius of $0.1345\ \mathrm{nm}$ and a density of $12.41\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Determine whether it has an FCC or a BCC crystal structure.
questions.solution_md:
### What is known

- $A_{\mathrm{Rh}} = 102.91\ \mathrm{g/mol}$
- $R = 0.1345\ \mathrm{nm} = 1.345\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$
- Density $\rho = 12.41\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$

### Test FCC

Assume FCC, so $n = 4$ and $a = 2R\sqrt{2}$:

$$a = 2\left(1.345\times10^{-8}\right)\sqrt{2} = 3.804\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$$

$$\rho = \frac{nA}{a^3 N_A} = \frac{4\times102.91}{\left(3.804\times10^{-8}\right)^3\times6.023\times10^{23}} = 12.41\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

### Conclusion

The calculated density is $12.41\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$, which is the value given in the problem statement. Therefore rhodium has the FCC crystal structure.

questions.title: Indices for four directions in a cubic unit cell
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T1 - Crystaline solids/Q and A - crystallographic direction and planes.pdf (question 1)
questions.body_md:
Determine the indices for the directions A, B, C and D shown in the following cubic unit cell.

![A cubic unit cell with four directions marked A, B, C and D](pack:l1-directions-cell)
questions.solution_md:
For each direction, take the head and tail coordinates in terms of the lattice parameters $a$, $b$ and $c$, subtract tail from head, then clear fractions to the smallest set of integers. A negative index is written with a bar over it.

### Direction A

| | $x$ | $y$ | $z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Head coordinates | $0a$ | $0b$ | $0c$ |
| Tail coordinates | $0a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
| Coordinate differences | $0a$ | $-b$ | $-c$ |
| Calculated $u$, $v$, $w$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $-1$ |

Enclosure: $[0\bar{1}\bar{1}]$

### Direction B

| | $x$ | $y$ | $z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Head coordinates | $0a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
| Tail coordinates | $a$ | $b/2$ | $c$ |
| Coordinate differences | $-a$ | $b/2$ | $0$ |
| Calculated $u$, $v$, $w$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Enclosure: $[\bar{2}10]$

### Direction C

| | $x$ | $y$ | $z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Head coordinates | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
| Tail coordinates | $a/2$ | $b/2$ | $0c$ |
| Coordinate differences | $a/2$ | $b/2$ | $c$ |
| Calculated $u$, $v$, $w$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Enclosure: $[112]$

### Direction D

| | $x$ | $y$ | $z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Head coordinates | $a$ | $b/2$ | $0c$ |
| Tail coordinates | $a/2$ | $0b$ | $c$ |
| Coordinate differences | $a/2$ | $b/2$ | $-c$ |
| Calculated $u$, $v$, $w$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-2$ |

Enclosure: $[11\bar{2}]$

questions.title: Miller indices for two planes in a cubic unit cell
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T1 - Crystaline solids/Q and A - crystallographic direction and planes.pdf (question 2)
questions.body_md:
Determine the Miller indices for the planes A and B shown in the following unit cell.

![A cubic unit cell with two shaded planes marked A and B](pack:l1-planes-cell)
questions.solution_md:
For each plane, read its intercepts on the three axes, express them as multiples of $a$, $b$ and $c$, take reciprocals, and reduce to the smallest integers. Where a plane passes through the origin, move the origin one unit cell first.

### Plane A

Move the origin of the coordinate system one unit cell distance upward along the $z$ axis. This gives a $(32\bar{2})$ plane:

| | $x$ | $y$ | $z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intercepts | $a/3$ | $b/2$ | $-c/2$ |
| Intercepts in terms of $a$, $b$, $c$ | $1/3$ | $1/2$ | $-1/2$ |
| Reciprocals of intercepts | $3$ | $2$ | $-2$ |
| Reduction | not necessary | | |

Enclosure: $(32\bar{2})$

### Plane B

Move the origin of the coordinate system one unit cell distance along the $x$ axis. This gives a $(\bar{1}01)$ plane:

| | $x$ | $y$ | $z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intercepts | $-a/2$ | $\infty b$ | $c/2$ |
| Intercepts in terms of $a$, $b$, $c$ | $-1/2$ | $\infty$ | $1/2$ |
| Reciprocals of intercepts | $-2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| Reduction | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Enclosure: $(\bar{1}01)$

questions.title: Lithium content of an aluminium-lithium aircraft skin
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T2 - Imperfection in solids/Sample questions - Imperfection of solids.pdf (question 1)
questions.body_md: Aluminum-lithium alloys have been developed by the aircraft industry to reduce the weight and improve the performance of its aircrafts. A commercial aircraft skin material having a density of $2.47\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ is desired. Compute the concentration of Li (in wt%) that is required.
questions.solution_md:
### What is known

$\rho_{\mathrm{Li}} = 0.534\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$; $\rho_{\mathrm{Al}} = 2.71\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$; $\rho_{\mathrm{alloy}} = 2.47\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$

### Start from the alloy density relation

For a two-element alloy the density follows from the weight percentages of its constituents:

$$\rho_{\mathrm{alloy}} = \frac{100}{\left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{Li}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Li}}}\right) + \left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{Al}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Al}}}\right)}$$

### Eliminate the second unknown

There are only two components, so $C_{\mathrm{Al}} = 100 - C_{\mathrm{Li}}$:

$$\rho_{\mathrm{alloy}} = \frac{100}{\left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{Li}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Li}}}\right) + \left(\frac{100 - C_{\mathrm{Li}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Al}}}\right)}$$

### Rearrange for the lithium content

$$\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{Al}} C_{\mathrm{Li}} + 100\rho_{\mathrm{Li}} - \rho_{\mathrm{Li}} C_{\mathrm{Li}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Li}}\rho_{\mathrm{Al}}} = \frac{100}{\rho_{\mathrm{alloy}}}$$

$$C_{\mathrm{Li}} = \frac{100\,\rho_{\mathrm{Li}}\left(\rho_{\mathrm{Al}} - \rho_{\mathrm{alloy}}\right)}{\rho_{\mathrm{alloy}}\left(\rho_{\mathrm{Al}} - \rho_{\mathrm{Li}}\right)}$$

### Substitute

$$C_{\mathrm{Li}} = \frac{100\,(0.534)(2.71 - 2.47)}{2.47\,(2.71 - 0.534)} = 2.38\ \mathrm{wt\%}$$

questions.title: Approximate density of a Ti-6Al-4V alloy
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T2 - Imperfection in solids/Sample questions - Imperfection of solids.pdf (question 2)
questions.body_md: Determine the approximate density of a Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy that has a composition of 90 wt% Ti, 6 wt% Al and 4 wt% V.
questions.solution_md:
### The relation for a multi-component alloy

$$\rho_{\mathrm{average}} = \frac{100}{\left(\frac{C_1}{\rho_1}\right) + \left(\frac{C_2}{\rho_2}\right) + \left(\frac{C_3}{\rho_3}\right)}$$

### Look up the constituent densities

From tables, $\rho_{\mathrm{Ti}} = 4.51\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$; $\rho_{\mathrm{Al}} = 2.71\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$; $\rho_{\mathrm{V}} = 6.1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$

### Substitute

$$\rho_{\mathrm{average}} = \frac{100}{\left(\frac{90}{4.51}\right) + \left(\frac{6}{2.71}\right) + \left(\frac{4}{6.1}\right)} = 4.38\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

questions.title: Vacancies per cubic metre in iron at 850 °C
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T2 - Imperfection in solids/Sample questions - Imperfection of solids.pdf (question 3)
questions.body_md: Calculate the number of vacancies per cubic meter in iron at $850\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The energy for vacancy formation is $1.08\ \mathrm{eV/atom}$. The density and atomic weight for Fe are $7.65\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ and $55.85\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, respectively.
questions.solution_md:
### Which equations are needed

Determining the number of vacancies per cubic metre in iron at $850\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($1123\ \mathrm{K}$) requires the equilibrium vacancy relation together with the expression for the number of atomic sites per unit volume:

$$N_v = N \exp\left(-\frac{Q_v}{kT}\right) = \frac{N_A \rho_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{A_{\mathrm{Fe}}} \exp\left(-\frac{Q_v}{kT}\right)$$

### Substitute the given values

$$N_v = \frac{\left(6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{atoms/mol}\right)\left(7.65\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\right)}{55.85\ \mathrm{g/mol}} \exp\left[-\frac{1.08\ \mathrm{eV/atom}}{\left(8.62\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/atom\text{-}K}\right)\left(850\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273\ \mathrm{K}\right)}\right]$$

### Result

$$N_v = 1.18\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 1.18\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$$

Note the unit conversion at the end: the density was given per cubic centimetre, and the question asks per cubic metre.

questions.title: Fraction of vacant sites in lead at two temperatures
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T2 - Imperfection in solids/Sample questions - Imperfection of solids.pdf (question 4)
questions.body_md:
(a) Calculate the fraction of atom sites that are vacant for lead at its melting temperature of $327\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($600\ \mathrm{K}$). Assume an energy for vacancy formation of $0.55\ \mathrm{eV/atom}$.

(b) Repeat this calculation at room temperature ($298\ \mathrm{K}$).

(c) What is the ratio of $N_v/N(600\ \mathrm{K})$ and $N_v/N(298\ \mathrm{K})$?
questions.solution_md:
### (a) At the melting temperature

To compute the fraction of atom sites that are vacant in lead at $600\ \mathrm{K}$ we use the equilibrium vacancy relation. As stated in the problem, $Q_v = 0.55\ \mathrm{eV/atom}$. Thus,

$$\frac{N_v}{N} = \exp\left(-\frac{Q_v}{kT}\right) = \exp\left[-\frac{0.55\ \mathrm{eV/atom}}{\left(8.62\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/atom\text{-}K}\right)\left(600\ \mathrm{K}\right)}\right] = 2.41\times10^{-5}$$

### (b) At room temperature

We repeat this computation at room temperature ($298\ \mathrm{K}$), as follows:

$$\frac{N_v}{N} = \exp\left[-\frac{0.55\ \mathrm{eV/atom}}{\left(8.62\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/atom\text{-}K}\right)\left(298\ \mathrm{K}\right)}\right] = 5.03\times10^{-10}$$

### (c) The ratio

$$\frac{N_v/N(600\ \mathrm{K})}{N_v/N(298\ \mathrm{K})} = \frac{2.41\times10^{-5}}{5.03\times10^{-10}} = 4.79\times10^{4}$$

Nearly five orders of magnitude between room temperature and the melting point, from a term that sits in an exponential: this is why vacancy-driven processes are negligible cold and dominant hot.

questions.title: Atom percent of a 30 wt% Zn brass
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T2 - Imperfection in solids/Sample questions - Imperfection of solids.pdf (question 5)
questions.body_md: What is the composition, in atom percent, of an alloy that consists of 30 wt% Zn and 70 wt% Cu?
questions.solution_md:
### The weight-percent to atom-percent conversion

For a two-element alloy,

$$C'_1 = \frac{C_1 A_2}{C_1 A_2 + C_2 A_1}\times 100$$

### Atomic weights

$A_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 63.55\ \mathrm{g/mol}$ and $A_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 65.41\ \mathrm{g/mol}$.

### Substitute for copper

$$C'_{\mathrm{Cu}} = \frac{(70)(65.41)}{(70)(65.41) + (30)(63.55)}\times 100 = 70.6\ \mathrm{at\%}$$

### And zinc by difference

$$C'_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 100 - 70.6 = 29.4\ \mathrm{at\%}$$

The two percentages are close to the weight percentages here because copper and zinc have nearly the same atomic weight.

questions.title: Atom percent of a tin-lead alloy given its masses
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T2 - Imperfection in solids/Sample questions - Imperfection of solids.pdf (question 6)
questions.body_md: What is the composition, in atom percent, of an alloy that contains 98 g tin and 65 g of lead?
questions.solution_md:
### Work in moles

The masses are given directly, so go straight to the number of moles of each element rather than through weight percent:

$$n_{m1} = \frac{m_1}{A_1}$$

### Atomic weights

$A_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 118.71\ \mathrm{g/mol}$ and $A_{\mathrm{Pb}} = 207.2\ \mathrm{g/mol}$.

### Moles of each

$$n_{m\mathrm{Sn}} = \frac{98\ \mathrm{g}}{118.71\ \mathrm{g/mol}} = 0.826\ \mathrm{mol}$$

$$n_{m\mathrm{Pb}} = \frac{65\ \mathrm{g}}{207.2\ \mathrm{g/mol}} = 0.314\ \mathrm{mol}$$

### Atom percent

$$C'_{\mathrm{Sn}} = \frac{n_{m\mathrm{Sn}}}{n_{m\mathrm{Sn}} + n_{m\mathrm{Pb}}}\times 100 = \frac{0.826}{0.826 + 0.314}\times 100 = 72.5\ \mathrm{at\%}$$

$$C'_{\mathrm{Pb}} = 100 - 72.5 = 27.5\ \mathrm{at\%}$$

Lead is the heavier atom, so its share by atoms is well below its share by mass.

questions.title: Crystal structure of a hypothetical A-B alloy
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T2 - Imperfection in solids/Sample questions in imperfection of solids.docx (question 7)
questions.body_md: Some hypothetical alloy is composed of 25 wt% of metal A and 75 wt% of metal B. If the densities of metals A and B are $6.17\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ and $8.00\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ respectively, and their respective atomic weights are $171.3\ \mathrm{g/mol}$ and $162.0\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, determine whether the crystal structure for this alloy is simple cubic, face-centered cubic, or body-centered cubic. Assume a unit cell edge length of $0.332\ \mathrm{nm}$.
questions.solution_md:
### The idea

Use the density relation, but with the *average* density and average atomic weight of the alloy in place of a pure element's, and solve it for $n$, the number of atoms per unit cell. The unit cell is cubic in all three candidate structures, so $V_C = a^3$:

$$\rho_{\mathrm{ave}} = \frac{n A_{\mathrm{ave}}}{a^3 N_A}$$

### What $n$ tells you

For $n = 1$ the structure is simple cubic, while values of 2 and 4 mean BCC and FCC respectively.

### Average density and atomic weight

$$\rho_{\mathrm{ave}} = \frac{100}{\frac{C_A}{\rho_A} + \frac{C_B}{\rho_B}} = \frac{100}{\frac{25}{6.17} + \frac{75}{8.00}} = 7.45\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

$$A_{\mathrm{ave}} = \frac{100}{\frac{C_A}{A_A} + \frac{C_B}{A_B}} = \frac{100}{\frac{25}{171.3} + \frac{75}{162.0}} = 164.2\ \mathrm{g/mol}$$

### Solve for $n$

$$n = \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{ave}} a^3 N_A}{A_{\mathrm{ave}}} = \frac{(7.45)\left(3.32\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^3\left(6.022\times10^{23}\right)}{164.2} = 1.00\ \mathrm{atom/unit\ cell}$$

### Conclusion

On the basis of this value, the crystal structure is simple cubic.

questions.title: Which elements form solid solutions with copper
questions.source: 02 - Lectures/L2 - Imperfections in solids/Sample questions - Imperfections.pdf (question 4)
questions.body_md:
Which of these elements would you expect to form the following with copper:

- **(a)** A substitutional solid solution having complete solubility
- **(b)** A substitutional solid solution of incomplete solubility
- **(c)** An interstitial solid solution

| Element | Atomic radius (nm) | Crystal structure | Electronegativity | Valence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cu | 0.1278 | FCC | 1.9 | +2 |
| C | 0.071 | | | |
| H | 0.046 | | | |
| O | 0.060 | | | |
| Ag | 0.1445 | FCC | 1.9 | +1 |
| Al | 0.1431 | FCC | 1.5 | +3 |
| Co | 0.1253 | HCP | 1.8 | +2 |
| Cr | 0.1249 | BCC | 1.6 | +3 |
| Fe | 0.1241 | BCC | 1.8 | +2 |
| Ni | 0.1246 | FCC | 1.8 | +2 |
| Pd | 0.1376 | FCC | 2.2 | +2 |
| Pt | 0.1387 | FCC | 2.2 | +2 |
| Zn | 0.1332 | HCP | 1.6 | +2 |
questions.solution_md:
### The rules being applied

Complete substitutional solubility asks for all four Hume-Rothery conditions at once: an atomic radius within about $\pm15\%$ of copper's, the same crystal structure, similar electronegativity, and the same valence. Failing any one of them leaves incomplete solubility. An atom much smaller than copper does not substitute at all; it fits between the copper atoms instead.

### The comparison

| Element | $\Delta R\%$ | Crystal structure | $\Delta$Electronegativity | Valence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cu | | FCC | | 2+ |
| C | $-44$ | | | |
| H | $-64$ | | | |
| O | $-53$ | | | |
| Ag | $+13$ | FCC | $0$ | 1+ |
| Al | $+12$ | FCC | $-0.4$ | 3+ |
| Co | $-2$ | HCP | $-0.1$ | 2+ |
| Cr | $-2$ | BCC | $-0.3$ | 3+ |
| Fe | $-3$ | BCC | $-0.1$ | 2+ |
| Ni | $-3$ | FCC | $-0.1$ | 2+ |
| Pd | $+8$ | FCC | $+0.3$ | 2+ |
| Pt | $+9$ | FCC | $+0.3$ | 2+ |
| Zn | $+4$ | HCP | $-0.3$ | 2+ |

### (a) Complete solubility

Ni, Pd and Pt meet all of the criteria and thus form substitutional solid solutions having complete solubility.

### (b) Incomplete solubility

Ag, Al, Co, Cr, Fe and Zn form substitutional solid solutions of incomplete solubility. All these metals have either BCC or HCP crystal structures, and/or the difference between their atomic radii and that for Cu is greater than $\pm15\%$, and/or have a valence different than 2+.

### (c) Interstitial solid solutions

C, H and O form interstitial solid solutions. These elements have atomic radii that are significantly smaller than the atomic radius of Cu.

questions.title: Hydrogen passing through a palladium sheet
questions.body_md: Compute the number of kilograms of hydrogen that pass per hour through a 6-mm thick sheet of palladium having an area of $0.25\ \mathrm{m^2}$ at $600\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume a diffusion coefficient of $1.7\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$, that the concentrations at the high and low pressure sides of the plate are 2.0 and $0.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ of hydrogen per cubic meter of palladium, and that steady state conditions have been attained.
questions.solution_md:
### Fick's first law

At steady state the diffusion flux is constant through the sheet:

$$J = \frac{M}{At} = -D\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta X}$$

where $M$ is the mass diffusing through area $A$ in time $t$.

### Rearrange for the mass

$$M = -D\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta X}At$$

### Substitute, with one hour as the time

$$M = -\left(1.7\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}\right)\left(\frac{-1.6\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}}{6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}}\right)\left(0.25\ \mathrm{m^2}\right)\left(3600\ \mathrm{s}\right) = 4.1\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}$$

The concentration difference is negative going down the gradient, and the minus sign in Fick's law turns it back into a positive mass, which is the sanity check worth making before trusting the arithmetic.

questions.title: Depth at which nitrogen reaches a given concentration
questions.body_md: A sheet of steel 1.5 mm thick has nitrogen atmospheres on both sides at $1200\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and is permitted to achieve a steady-state diffusion condition. The diffusion coefficient for nitrogen in steel at this temperature is $6\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$, and the diffusion flux is found to be $1.2\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{kg/m^2\text{-}s}$. Also, it is known that the concentration of nitrogen in the steel at the high-pressure surface is $4\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. How far into the sheet from this high-pressure side will the concentration be $2.0\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$? Assume a linear concentration profile.
questions.solution_md:
### Start from Fick's first law

This problem is solved by using Fick's first law in the form

$$J = -D\frac{C_A - C_B}{x_A - x_B}$$

### Solve for the unknown position

If we take $C_A$ to be the point at which the concentration of nitrogen is $4\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, then it becomes necessary to solve for $x_B$:

$$x_B = x_A + D\left(\frac{C_A - C_B}{J}\right)$$

### Substitute

Assume $x_A$ is zero at the surface, in which case

$$x_B = 0 + \left(6\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}\right)\left[\frac{4\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} - 2\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}}{1.2\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{kg/m^2\text{-}s}}\right] = 1\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{mm}$$

The sheet is 1.5 mm thick, so the answer falls inside it, which it had to for the linear profile to be the right assumption.

questions.title: Diffusion coefficient from a carburizing-decarburizing couple
questions.body_md:
A sheet of BCC iron 1 mm thick was exposed to a carburizing gas atmosphere on one side and a decarburizing atmosphere on the other side at $725\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. After having reached steady state, the iron was quickly cooled to room temperature. The carbon concentrations at the two surfaces of the sheet were determined to be 0.012 and 0.0075 wt%. Compute the diffusion coefficient if the diffusion flux is $1.4\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{kg/m^2\text{-}s}$.

Hint: convert the concentrations from weight percent to kilograms of carbon per cubic meter of iron.
questions.solution_md:
### First convert the concentrations

Fick's law needs mass per unit volume, not weight percent, so convert both surface concentrations using the mass-per-unit-volume relation. For 0.012 wt% C:

$$C''_C = \frac{C_C}{\frac{C_C}{\rho_C} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Fe}}}}\times 10^3 = \frac{0.012}{\frac{0.012}{2.25\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}} + \frac{99.988}{7.87\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}}}\times 10^3 = 0.944\ \mathrm{kg\ C/m^3}$$

### And the other surface

Similarly, for 0.0075 wt% C:

$$C''_C = \frac{0.0075}{\frac{0.0075}{2.25\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}} + \frac{99.9925}{7.87\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}}}\times 10^3 = 0.590\ \mathrm{kg\ C/m^3}$$

### Rearrange Fick's first law for $D$

$$D = -J\left[\frac{x_A - x_B}{C_A - C_B}\right]$$

### Substitute

$$D = -\left(1.40\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{kg/m^2\text{-}s}\right)\left[\frac{-10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}}{0.944\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} - 0.590\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}}\right] = 3.96\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$$

questions.title: Position of a carbon concentration after decarburization
questions.body_md: An FCC iron-carbon alloy initially containing 0.35 wt% C is exposed to an oxygen-rich and virtually carbon-free atmosphere at $1400\ \mathrm{K}$ ($1127\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Under these circumstances the carbon diffuses from the alloy and reacts at the surface with the oxygen in the atmosphere; that is, the carbon concentration at the surface position is maintained essentially at 0 wt% C. (This process of carbon depletion is termed decarburization.) At what position will the carbon concentration be 0.15 wt% after a 10-h treatment? The value of $D$ at $1400\ \mathrm{K}$ is $6.9\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$.
questions.solution_md:
### The non-steady-state solution

This problem asks for the position at which the carbon concentration is 0.15 wt% after a 10-h heat treatment at $1400\ \mathrm{K}$ when $C_0 = 0.35\ \mathrm{wt\%\ C}$. From the error-function solution to Fick's second law,

$$\frac{C_x - C_0}{C_s - C_0} = \frac{0.15 - 0.35}{0 - 0.35} = 0.5714 = 1 - \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right)$$

### Thus

$$\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right) = 0.4286$$

### Interpolate for $z$

Using tabulated values of the error function and linear interpolation:

| $z$ | $\mathrm{erf}(z)$ |
| --- | --- |
| 0.40 | 0.4284 |
| $z$ | 0.4286 |
| 0.45 | 0.4755 |

$$\frac{z - 0.40}{0.45 - 0.40} = \frac{0.4286 - 0.4284}{0.4755 - 0.4284}$$

$$z = 0.4002$$

### Solve for the position

$$x = 2(0.4002)\sqrt{Dt} = (0.8004)\sqrt{\left(6.9\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}\right)\left(3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{s}\right)} = 1.26\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1.26\ \mathrm{mm}$$

questions.title: Temperature giving a stated diffusion coefficient
questions.body_md: At what temperature will the diffusion coefficient for the diffusion of copper in nickel have a value of $6.5\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$? Use the tabulated diffusion data for copper in nickel.
questions.solution_md:
### The temperature dependence

$$D = D_0\exp\left(-\frac{Q_d}{RT}\right)$$

### Rearrange for temperature

Taking logarithms and solving for $T$:

$$T = \frac{Q_d}{R\ln\left(\frac{D_0}{D}\right)}$$

### Substitute the tabulated constants

For copper diffusing in nickel, $D_0 = 2.7\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$ and $Q_d = 256{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}$:

$$T = \frac{256{,}000}{(8.314)\ln\left(\frac{2.7\times10^{-5}}{6.5\times10^{-17}}\right)} = 1152\ \mathrm{K}$$

### In degrees Celsius

$$T = 1152\ \mathrm{K} - 273 = 879\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$$

questions.title: Activation energy for iron diffusing in nickel
questions.body_md:
The diffusion coefficients for iron in nickel are given at two temperatures:

| $T$ (K) | $D$ (m²/s) |
| --- | --- |
| 1273 | $9.4\times10^{-16}$ |
| 1473 | $2.4\times10^{-14}$ |

(a) Determine the values of $D_0$ and the activation energy $Q_d$.

(b) What is the magnitude of $D$ at $1100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($1373\ \mathrm{K}$)?
questions.solution_md:
### (a) Two equations, two unknowns

Writing the temperature dependence at each of the two temperatures and dividing one by the other eliminates $D_0$:

$$\ln\left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right) = -\frac{Q_d}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

### Solve for the activation energy

$$Q_d = -R\,\frac{\ln\left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)}{\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}} = -(8.314)\,\frac{\ln\left(\frac{2.4\times10^{-14}}{9.4\times10^{-16}}\right)}{\frac{1}{1473} - \frac{1}{1273}} = 2.53\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J/mol}$$

### Then back-substitute for $D_0$

$$D_0 = D_1\exp\left(\frac{Q_d}{RT_1}\right) = \left(9.4\times10^{-16}\right)\exp\left[\frac{2.53\times10^{5}}{(8.314)(1273)}\right] = 2.2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$$

### (b) Evaluate at 1373 K

$$D = \left(2.2\times10^{-5}\right)\exp\left[-\frac{2.53\times10^{5}}{(8.314)(1373)}\right] = 5.4\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$$

The answer sits between the two tabulated values, as it must, since 1373 K lies between 1273 K and 1473 K.

questions.title: Heating time for a silver-gold diffusion couple
questions.body_md: A diffusion couple composed of two silver-gold alloys is formed; these alloys have compositions of 98 wt% Ag-2 wt% Au and 95 wt% Ag-5 wt% Au. Determine the time this diffusion couple must be heated at $750\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($1023\ \mathrm{K}$) in order for the composition to be 2.5 wt% Au at the $50\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ position into the 2 wt% Au side of the diffusion couple. Preexponential and activation energy values for Au diffusion in Ag are $8.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$ and $202{,}100\ \mathrm{J/mol}$, respectively.
questions.solution_md:
### The diffusion-couple solution

For this silver-gold diffusion couple, with $C_1 = 5\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Au}$ and $C_2 = 2\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Au}$, we are asked for the diffusion time at $750\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ that gives a composition of 2.5 wt% Au at the $50\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ position:

$$C_x = \frac{C_1 + C_2}{2} + \frac{C_1 - C_2}{2}\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right)\right]$$

### Compute the diffusion coefficient first

It now becomes necessary to compute the diffusion coefficient at $750\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($1023\ \mathrm{K}$) given that $D_0 = 8.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$ and $Q_d = 202{,}100\ \mathrm{J/mol}$:

$$D = \left(8.5\times10^{-5}\right)\exp\left[-\frac{202{,}100\ \mathrm{J/mol}}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/mol\text{-}K})(1023\ \mathrm{K})}\right] = 4.03\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$$

### Reduce to an error function

Substituting the compositions into the expression above reduces it to

$$\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right) = 0.6667$$

### Interpolate for $z$

| $z$ | $\mathrm{erf}(z)$ |
| --- | --- |
| 0.650 | 0.6420 |
| $y$ | 0.6667 |
| 0.700 | 0.6778 |

from which $z = 0.6845$.

### Solve for the time

$$t = \frac{x^2}{4Dz^2} = \frac{\left(50\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}\right)^2}{4\left(4.03\times10^{-15}\right)(0.6845)^2} = 3.31\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{s} = 92\ \mathrm{h}$$

questions.title: Carburizing time to reach a carbon concentration at depth
questions.body_md: Determine the carburizing time necessary to achieve a carbon concentration of 0.30 wt% at a position 4 mm into an iron-carbon alloy that initially contains 0.10 wt% C. The surface concentration is to be maintained at 0.90 wt% C, and the treatment is to be conducted at $1100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Use the diffusion data for $\gamma$-Fe.
questions.solution_md:
### What is given

- Carbon concentration $C_x = 0.30\ \mathrm{wt\%}$
- $x = 4\ \mathrm{mm}$
- $C_0 = 0.10\ \mathrm{wt\%}$
- $C_s = 0.90\ \mathrm{wt\%\ C}$
- $T = 1100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and for $\gamma$-Fe this gives $D = 5.3\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$

### Set up the error-function solution

$$\frac{C_x - C_0}{C_s - C_0} = 1 - \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right)$$

$$\frac{0.30 - 0.10}{0.90 - 0.10} = 0.2500 = 1 - \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right)$$

$$\mathrm{erf}(z) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75$$

### Interpolate for $z$

| $\mathrm{erf}(z)$ | $z$ |
| --- | --- |
| 0.7421 | 0.80 |
| 0.75 | $z$ |
| 0.7707 | 0.85 |

$$\frac{z - 0.80}{0.85 - 0.80} = \frac{0.75 - 0.7421}{0.7707 - 0.7421}$$

$$z = 0.814 = \frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}$$

### Solve for the time

$$t = \frac{x^2}{4Dz^2} = \frac{\left(4\times10^{-3}\right)^2}{4\left(5.3\times10^{-11}\right)(0.814)^2} = 113{,}903\ \mathrm{s} = 31.6\ \mathrm{hours}$$

questions.title: Elastic strain in an aluminium bar
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (question 1)
questions.body_md: A specimen of aluminum having a rectangular cross section $10\ \mathrm{mm}\times12.7\ \mathrm{mm}$ is pulled in tension with $35{,}500\ \mathrm{N}$ force, producing only elastic deformation. Calculate the resulting strain.
questions.solution_md:
### The cross-sectional area

The cross-sectional area is just $(10\ \mathrm{mm})\times(12.7\ \mathrm{mm}) = 127\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 1.27\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

### The elastic modulus

The elastic modulus for Al is tabulated as $69\ \mathrm{GPa}$ (or $69\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$).

### Combine the definitions of stress and Hooke's law

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{F}{A_0 E}$$

### Substitute

$$\varepsilon = \frac{35{,}500\ \mathrm{N}}{\left(1.27\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}\right)\left(69\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N/m^2}\right)} = 4.1\times10^{-3}$$

Strain is dimensionless, which is the check to make: if units survive to the answer, something has gone wrong earlier.

questions.title: Maximum length of a titanium specimen under an elongation limit
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (question 2)
questions.body_md: A cylindrical specimen of a titanium alloy having an elastic modulus of $107\ \mathrm{GPa}$ and an original diameter of $3.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ will experience only elastic deformation when a tensile load of $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ is applied. Compute the maximum length of the specimen before deformation if the maximum allowable elongation is $0.42\ \mathrm{mm}$.
questions.solution_md:
### The cross-sectional area

For a cylindrical specimen the cross-sectional area is

$$A_0 = \pi\left(\frac{d_0}{2}\right)^2$$

where $d_0$ is the original diameter.

### Combine stress, strain and Hooke's law

$$\sigma = E\varepsilon\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{F}{A_0} = E\,\frac{\Delta l}{l_0}$$

### Solve for the original length

$$l_0 = \frac{\Delta l\,E\,A_0}{F} = \frac{\Delta l\,E\,\pi\left(\frac{d_0}{2}\right)^2}{F}$$

### Substitute

$$l_0 = \frac{\left(0.42\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\right)\left(107\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N/m^2}\right)\pi\left(\frac{3.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}}{2}\right)^2}{2000\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.255\ \mathrm{m} = 255\ \mathrm{mm}$$

questions.title: Elongation and diameter change of an aluminium specimen
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (question 3)
questions.body_md:
A cylindrical specimen of aluminum having a diameter of $19\ \mathrm{mm}$ and length of $200\ \mathrm{mm}$ is deformed elastically in tension with a force of $48{,}800\ \mathrm{N}$. Using tabulated data, determine the following:

- **(a)** The amount by which this specimen will elongate in the direction of the applied stress.
- **(b)** The change in diameter of the specimen. Will the diameter increase or decrease?
questions.solution_md:
### (a) Combine stress, strain and Hooke's law

$$\sigma = E\varepsilon\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{F}{\pi\left(\frac{d_0^2}{4}\right)} = E\,\frac{\Delta l}{l_0}$$

### Solve for the elongation

Solving for $\Delta l$, and taking $E = 69\ \mathrm{GPa}$ for aluminium:

$$\Delta l = \frac{4Fl_0}{\pi d_0^2 E} = \frac{(4)(48{,}800\ \mathrm{N})\left(200\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\right)}{(\pi)\left(19\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\right)^2\left(69\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N/m^2}\right)} = 5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.50\ \mathrm{mm}$$

### (b) Bring in Poisson's ratio

$$\nu = -\frac{\varepsilon_x}{\varepsilon_z} = -\frac{\Delta d/d_0}{\Delta l/l_0}$$

### Solve for the diameter change

For aluminium, $\nu = 0.33$. Solving the above for $\Delta d$:

$$\Delta d = -\frac{\nu\,\Delta l\,d_0}{l_0} = -\frac{(0.33)(0.50\ \mathrm{mm})(19\ \mathrm{mm})}{200\ \mathrm{mm}} = -1.6\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mm}$$

The diameter will decrease. The negative sign is the physics, not a slip: a bar pulled longer gets thinner.

questions.title: Force producing a stated elastic reduction in diameter
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (question 4)
questions.body_md: A cylindrical bar of steel $10\ \mathrm{mm}$ in diameter is to be deformed elastically by application of a force along the bar axis. Using tabulated data, determine the force that will produce an elastic reduction of $3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mm}$ in the diameter.
questions.solution_md:
### Work backwards from the lateral strain

The reduction in diameter is a lateral strain, and Poisson's ratio connects it to the axial strain that caused it:

$$\varepsilon_z = -\frac{\Delta d}{\nu d_0}$$

### Substitute, with $\nu = 0.30$ for steel

$$\varepsilon_z = \frac{3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mm}}{(0.30)(10\ \mathrm{mm})} = 1\times10^{-3}$$

### Turn the axial strain into a force

$$F = \varepsilon_z A_0 E = \varepsilon_z \pi\left(\frac{d_0}{2}\right)^2 E$$

### Substitute, with $E = 207\ \mathrm{GPa}$ for steel

$$F = \left(1\times10^{-3}\right)\pi\left(5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\right)^2\left(207\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N/m^2}\right) = 16{,}250\ \mathrm{N}$$

questions.title: Which alloys can carry a rod's load within its limits
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (question 5)
questions.body_md:
A cylindrical rod $100\ \mathrm{mm}$ long and having a diameter of $10.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ is to be deformed using a tensile load of $27{,}500\ \mathrm{N}$. It must not experience either plastic deformation or a diameter reduction of more than $7.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mm}$. Of the materials listed as follows, which are possible candidates?

| Material | Modulus of elasticity (GPa) | Yield strength (MPa) | Poisson's ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Aluminum alloy | 70 | 200 | 0.33 |
| Brass alloy | 101 | 300 | 0.34 |
| Steel alloy | 207 | 400 | 0.30 |
| Titanium alloy | 107 | 650 | 0.34 |
questions.solution_md:
### There are two separate criteria

A candidate has to pass both: no plastic deformation, and a diameter reduction inside the limit. Test them one at a time.

### The applied stress

$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0} = \frac{27{,}500\ \mathrm{N}}{\pi\left(5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\right)^2} = 350\ \mathrm{MPa}$$

### First criterion: the yield strength must exceed it

The aluminium alloy (200 MPa) and the brass alloy (300 MPa) both yield under 350 MPa, so they are out. The steel (400 MPa) and the titanium (650 MPa) survive.

### Second criterion: the diameter reduction

$$\Delta d = -\frac{\nu\,\sigma\,d_0}{E}$$

For the steel:

$$\Delta d = \frac{(0.30)(350\ \mathrm{MPa})(10\ \mathrm{mm})}{207\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{MPa}} = 5.1\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mm}$$

For the titanium:

$$\Delta d = \frac{(0.34)(350\ \mathrm{MPa})(10\ \mathrm{mm})}{107\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{MPa}} = 1.1\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mm}$$

### Conclusion

The steel's reduction is inside the $7.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mm}$ limit and the titanium's is not, despite the titanium having much the higher yield strength. The steel is the candidate. The stiffer material wins the second criterion, and stiffness and strength are not the same property.

questions.title: Length and yield load of a structural steel component
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (unnumbered question, structural component)
questions.body_md:
A structural component, $2.54\ \mathrm{cm}$ in diameter and $6.1\ \mathrm{m}$ long, is made of a special steel alloy which has the following properties: Young's modulus $= 193\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{MPa}$; tensile strength $= 1309\ \mathrm{MPa}$; yield strength $= 1034\ \mathrm{MPa}$; and ductility $= 15\%\mathrm{EL}$.

- **(a)** What will be the length of the bar under a load of $334\ \mathrm{kN}$?
- **(b)** At what approximate load will the bar be stretched permanently?
questions.solution_md:
### (a) The cross-sectional area

$$A = \pi\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2 = \pi\left(\frac{0.0254\ \mathrm{m}}{2}\right)^2 = 5.067\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$$

### The stress

$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{334\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N}}{5.067\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}} = 659\ \mathrm{MPa}$$

This is below the $1034\ \mathrm{MPa}$ yield strength, so the deformation is elastic and Hooke's law applies.

### The strain

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{659\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}}{193\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{Pa}} = 0.003415$$

### The stretched length

$$L = L_0(1 + \varepsilon) = (6.1\ \mathrm{m})(1.003415) = 6.12\ \mathrm{m}$$

### (b) Permanent stretch begins at yield

Permanent strain occurs once the stress reaches the yield strength of $1034\ \mathrm{MPa}$:

$$F = A\sigma_y = \left(5.067\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}\right)\left(1034\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}\right) = 524{,}000\ \mathrm{N} \approx 524\ \mathrm{kN}$$

questions.title: Flexural strength and deflection in a three-point bend test
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (unnumbered question, three-point bending)
questions.body_md:
A three-point bending test is performed on a ceramic ($\mathrm{MgAl_2O_4}$) specimen having a rectangular cross section of height $d = 3.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ and width $b = 9\ \mathrm{mm}$; the distance between support points is $25\ \mathrm{mm}$.

- **(a)** Compute the flexural strength if the load at fracture is $350\ \mathrm{N}$.
- **(b)** The point of maximum deflection $\Delta y$ occurs at the centre of the specimen and is described by

$$\Delta y = \frac{FL^3}{48EI}$$

where $E$ is the modulus of elasticity and $I$ is the cross-sectional moment of inertia. Compute $\Delta y$ at a load of $310\ \mathrm{N}$.
questions.solution_md:
### (a) Flexural strength for a rectangular cross section

$$\sigma_{fs} = \frac{3F_f L}{2bd^2} = \frac{3(350\ \mathrm{N})(0.025\ \mathrm{m})}{2(0.009\ \mathrm{m})(0.0038\ \mathrm{m})^2} = 101\ \mathrm{MPa}$$

### (b) The moment of inertia

For a rectangular cross section,

$$I = \frac{bd^3}{12} = \frac{(0.009)(0.0038)^3}{12} = 4.115\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^4}$$

### The modulus

The value of the modulus $E$ for this ceramic is $260\ \mathrm{GPa}$.

### The deflection at 310 N

$$\Delta y = \frac{FL^3}{48EI} = \frac{(310)(0.025)^3}{48\left(260\times10^{9}\right)\left(4.115\times10^{-11}\right)} = 9.4\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$$

Under ten micrometres of deflection at a load most of the way to fracture: a ceramic is stiff, and it is that stiffness with no plastic reserve behind it that makes the failure sudden.

questions.title: Brinell hardness and indentation diameter
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (unnumbered question, Brinell hardness)
questions.body_md:
A $10\ \mathrm{mm}$ diameter Brinell hardness indenter produced an indentation of $2.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ in diameter in a steel alloy when a load of $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ was used.

- **(a)** What is the Brinell Hardness (HB) of this material?
- **(b)** What would be the diameter of the indentation for a hardness of $300\ \mathrm{HB}$ for a $500\ \mathrm{kg}$ applied load?
questions.solution_md:
### (a) The Brinell relation

$$HB = \frac{2P}{\pi D\left(D - \sqrt{D^2 - d^2}\right)}$$

where $P$ is the load in kg, $D$ the indenter diameter and $d$ the indentation diameter, both in mm.

### Substitute

$$HB = \frac{2(1000)}{\pi(10)\left(10 - \sqrt{10^2 - 2.5^2}\right)} = 200.48$$

### (b) Rearrange for the indentation diameter

$$d = \sqrt{D^2 - \left(D - \frac{2P}{(HB)\pi D}\right)^2}$$

### Substitute

$$d = \sqrt{10^2 - \left(10 - \frac{2(500)}{(300)\pi(10)}\right)^2} = 1.45\ \mathrm{mm}$$

A harder material under half the load leaves a smaller dent, which is the whole idea the test is built on.

questions.title: True stress at fracture for a copper wire
questions.source: 05 - Tutorials/T4 - Mechanical properties/Sample question - Mechanical properties 2.pdf (unnumbered question, copper wire)
questions.body_md: A copper wire has a nominal breaking strength of $300\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Its ductility is 77 percent reduction of area. Calculate the true stress at fracture.
questions.solution_md:
### What the two stresses mean

The nominal (engineering) strength divides the breaking load by the *original* area. True stress divides it by the area the wire actually has at fracture, which the necking has reduced.

### Use the reduction of area to get the final area

$$\%RA = \frac{A_0 - A_f}{A_0}\times 100\quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.77 = 1 - \frac{A_f}{A_0}$$

$$A_f = (1 - 0.77)A_0$$

### The breaking load is the same either way

$$F = \sigma A_0 = \left(300\times10^{6}\right)A_0$$

### Divide it by the true area

$$\sigma_{true} = \frac{F}{A_f} = \frac{\left(300\times10^{6}\right)A_0}{(1 - 0.77)A_0} = 1304\ \mathrm{MPa}$$

The original area cancels, so the answer never needed the wire's actual size. A very ductile metal necks hard, and its true fracture stress is several times the number the tensile test reports.

questions.title: Reading a brass stress-strain curve
questions.source: 02 - Lectures/L4 - Mechanical Properties/L4 - Mechanical properties.pdf (worked example, slides 29 to 32)
questions.body_md:
The stress-strain behaviour for a specimen of brass is presented here. Determine:

- **(a)** the modulus of elasticity,
- **(b)** the yield strength at a strain offset of 0.002,
- **(c)** the maximum load that can be sustained by a cylindrical specimen having an original diameter of $12.8\ \mathrm{mm}$,
- **(d)** the change in length of a specimen originally $250\ \mathrm{mm}$ long that is subjected to a tensile stress of $345\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

![Engineering stress-strain curve for a brass specimen, with the tensile strength, the 0.002 offset yield strength, and point A at 345 MPa marked](pack:l4-brass-stress-strain)
questions.solution_md:
### (a) The modulus of elasticity

The modulus of elasticity is the slope of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve:

$$E = \mathrm{slope} = \frac{\Delta\sigma}{\Delta\varepsilon} = \frac{\sigma_2 - \sigma_1}{\varepsilon_2 - \varepsilon_1} = \frac{(150 - 0)\ \mathrm{MPa}}{0.0016 - 0} = 93.8\ \mathrm{GPa}$$

### (b) The yield strength

The 0.002 strain offset is drawn parallel to the linear section of the stress-strain curve. Where it intersects the curve, you obtain the yield strength. In this case $250\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

### (c) The maximum load

The maximum load is calculated from the engineering stress equation, with $\sigma$ the maximum tensile strength of $450\ \mathrm{MPa}$ read off the curve:

$$F = \sigma A_0 = \sigma\pi\left(\frac{d_0}{2}\right)^2 = \left(450\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N/m^2}\right)\pi\left(\frac{12.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}}{2}\right)^2 = 57{,}900\ \mathrm{N}$$

### (d) The change in length

$\Delta l = \varepsilon l_0$. Locate $\varepsilon$ on the curve for $\sigma = 345\ \mathrm{MPa}$: it is represented by point A, for a value $\varepsilon = 0.06$. With $l_0 = 250\ \mathrm{mm}$:

$$\Delta l = \varepsilon l_0 = (0.06)(250\ \mathrm{mm}) = 15\ \mathrm{mm}$$

questions.title: Nickel to add to keep a copper melt fully liquid
questions.body_md:
You're working at a metal casting workshop making specialized copper-nickel alloys for high-temperature industrial equipment. You have $5.66\ \mathrm{kg}$ of copper ready in your crucible. How many kilograms of nickel should you add to ensure the mixture stays fully liquid at $1200\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for proper casting?

![The copper-nickel phase diagram, temperature against wt% Ni](pack:l5-cu-ni)
questions.solution_md:
### Read the liquidus off the diagram

According to the copper-nickel phase diagram, the composition at the $1200\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ liquidus temperature is about 20 wt% Ni. Any more nickel than that and the melt would begin to solidify at this temperature.

### Set up the composition relation

If we let $m_{\mathrm{Ni}}$ represent the mass of nickel required, then the weight percent of nickel is

$$C_{\mathrm{Ni}} = \frac{m_{\mathrm{Ni}}}{m_{\mathrm{Ni}} + m_{\mathrm{Cu}}}\times 100 = 20$$

### Substitute and solve

$$\frac{m_{\mathrm{Ni}}}{m_{\mathrm{Ni}} + 5.66\ \mathrm{kg}} = 0.20$$

$$m_{\mathrm{Ni}} = 1.42\ \mathrm{kg}$$

questions.title: Phases and phase compositions for eight alloys
questions.body_md:
Cite the phases that are present and the phase compositions for the following alloys:

- **(a)** 90 wt% Zn-10 wt% Cu at $400\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- **(b)** 75 wt% Sn-25 wt% Pb at $175\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- **(c)** 55 wt% Ag-45 wt% Cu at $900\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- **(d)** 30 wt% Pb-70 wt% Mg at $425\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- **(e)** $2.12\ \mathrm{kg}$ Zn and $1.88\ \mathrm{kg}$ Cu at $500\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- **(f)** $37\ \mathrm{lb_m}$ Pb and $6.5\ \mathrm{lb_m}$ Mg at $400\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- **(g)** $8.2\ \mathrm{mol}$ Ni and $4.3\ \mathrm{mol}$ Cu at $1250\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- **(h)** $4.5\ \mathrm{mol}$ Sn and $0.45\ \mathrm{mol}$ Pb at $200\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$

![The copper-zinc phase diagram, temperature against wt% Zn](pack:l5-cu-zn)

![The lead-tin phase diagram, with the 183 degree C eutectic isotherm at 61.9 wt% Sn](pack:l5-pb-sn)

![The copper-silver phase diagram, with the 779 degree C eutectic isotherm at 71.9 wt% Ag](pack:l5-ag-cu)

![The magnesium-lead phase diagram, temperature against wt% Pb](pack:l5-mg-pb)

![The copper-nickel phase diagram, temperature against wt% Ni](pack:l5-cu-ni)
questions.solution_md:
### The method, once

Locate the point on the relevant diagram. If it lies in a single-phase field, that phase is present and its composition is the alloy's own. If it lies in a two-phase field, construct a tie line at that temperature: where it meets each phase boundary gives that phase's composition.

### (a) 90 wt% Zn-10 wt% Cu at 400 °C

The point lies within the $\varepsilon + \eta$ phase field. A tie line at $400\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ meets the $\varepsilon-(\varepsilon + \eta)$ boundary at 87 wt% Zn and the $(\varepsilon + \eta)-\eta$ boundary at 97 wt% Zn. Thus

$$C_\varepsilon = 87\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Zn}\text{-}13\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Cu}\qquadC_\eta = 97\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Zn}\text{-}3\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Cu}$$

### (b) 75 wt% Sn-25 wt% Pb at 175 °C

The point lies within the $\alpha + \beta$ phase field. The tie line meets the $\alpha-(\alpha + \beta)$ boundary at 16 wt% Sn and the $(\alpha + \beta)-\beta$ boundary at 97 wt% Sn:

$$C_\alpha = 16\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}\text{-}84\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}\qquadC_\beta = 97\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}\text{-}3\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$$

### (c) 55 wt% Ag-45 wt% Cu at 900 °C

The point lies within the liquid phase field. Therefore only the liquid phase is present, and its composition is the alloy's own: 55 wt% Ag-45 wt% Cu.

### (d) 30 wt% Pb-70 wt% Mg at 425 °C

Only the $\alpha$ phase is present; its composition is 30 wt% Pb-70 wt% Mg.

### (e) 2.12 kg Zn and 1.88 kg Cu at 500 °C

First convert the masses to a composition:

$$C_{\mathrm{Zn}} = \frac{2.12}{2.12 + 1.88}\times 100 = 53\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Zn}$$

The point lies within the $\beta + \gamma$ phase field, and the tie line at $500\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ gives

$$C_\beta = 49\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Zn}\text{-}51\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Cu}\qquadC_\gamma = 58\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Zn}\text{-}42\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Cu}$$

### (f) 37 lbm Pb and 6.5 lbm Mg at 400 °C

$$C_{\mathrm{Mg_2Pb}} = 81\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}\text{-}19\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Mg}\qquadC_L = 93\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}\text{-}7\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Mg}$$

### (g) 8.2 mol Ni and 4.3 mol Cu at 1250 °C

Only the $\alpha$ phase is present; its composition is 63.8 wt% Ni-36.2 wt% Cu.

### (h) 4.5 mol Sn and 0.45 mol Pb at 200 °C

Convert moles to masses, then to weight percent:

$$m_{\mathrm{Sn}} = (4.5)(118.71) = 534\ \mathrm{g}\qquadm_{\mathrm{Pb}} = (0.45)(207.2) = 93.2\ \mathrm{g}$$

$$C_{\mathrm{Sn}} = \frac{534}{534 + 93.2}\times 100 = 85.1\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}$$

The point lies within the $\beta + L$ phase field, and the tie line at $200\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ gives

$$C_\beta = 97.5\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}\text{-}2.5\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}\qquadC_L = 74\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}\text{-}26\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$$

questions.title: Slow cooling of a 50 wt% Pb-50 wt% Mg alloy
questions.body_md:
A 50 wt% Pb-50 wt% Mg alloy is slowly cooled from $700\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $400\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

- **(a)** At what temperature does the first solid phase form?
- **(b)** What is the composition of this solid phase?
- **(c)** At what temperature does the liquid solidify?
- **(d)** What is the composition of this last remaining liquid phase?

![The magnesium-lead phase diagram, temperature against wt% Pb](pack:l5-mg-pb)
questions.solution_md:
### Construct the composition line

Draw a vertical line on the Mg-Pb diagram at 50 wt% Pb and follow it downward from $700\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

### (a) First solid

Upon cooling from $700\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the first solid phase forms where the vertical line crosses the $L-(\alpha + L)$ phase boundary, at about $560\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

### (b) Composition of that solid

Construct a tie line across the $\alpha + L$ region at $560\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$; its intersection with the $\alpha-(\alpha + L)$ boundary gives 21 wt% Pb-79 wt% Mg.

### (c) Complete solidification

Complete solidification occurs where the same vertical line meets the eutectic isotherm, at about $465\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

### (d) The last liquid

The composition of the last liquid remaining before complete solidification is the eutectic composition, about 67 wt% Pb-33 wt% Mg.

questions.title: Getting a solder batch half melted, two ways
questions.body_md:
You're working at a soldering facility that manufactures specialized lead-tin solder joints. You have a $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ batch of solder that's 90% lead and 10% tin, currently heated to $250\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in your temperature-controlled pot. For your next manufacturing process, you need exactly half of the solder to be melted while the other half remains solid; this specific semi-solid state is crucial for the joint quality.

You can achieve this two ways: (1) simply adjusting the temperature of your current mixture, or (2) keeping the temperature at $250\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ but adding more tin to the mix.

- **(a)** If you choose to adjust temperature, what should you set your heating pot to?
- **(b)** If you prefer keeping it at $250\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, how many grams of tin should you add to your current $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ batch?

![The lead-tin phase diagram, with the 183 degree C eutectic isotherm at 61.9 wt% Sn](pack:l5-pb-sn)
questions.solution_md:
### (a) Find the temperature by trial and error

Half melted means $W_\alpha = W_L = 0.5$, and by the lever rule that happens exactly where the tie-line lengths on both sides of the alloy composition are equal. On the Pb-Sn diagram, move vertically at 10 wt% Sn through the $\alpha + L$ region until that is true. This occurs at approximately $295\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

### (b) Or change the composition instead

At $250\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, within the $\alpha + L$ phase region, the tie line gives

$$C_\alpha = 14\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}\text{-}86\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}\qquadC_L = 34\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}\text{-}66\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$$

### The composition that splits the tie line evenly

Let $C_0$ be the new alloy composition giving $W_\alpha = W_L = 0.5$. Equal mass fractions put $C_0$ at the midpoint of the tie line:

$$C_0 = \frac{C_\alpha + C_L}{2} = \frac{14 + 34}{2} = 24\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}$$

### How much tin that means adding

The amount of Sn in the original alloy is $(0.10)(1.5\ \mathrm{kg}) = 0.15\ \mathrm{kg}$. Letting $m_{\mathrm{Sn}}$ be the mass added,

$$\frac{0.15 + m_{\mathrm{Sn}}}{1.5 + m_{\mathrm{Sn}}} = 0.24$$

$$m_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.276\ \mathrm{kg} = 276\ \mathrm{g}$$

Note that the tin added counts in both the numerator and the denominator, which is why this is not simply 24% of 1.5 kg.

questions.title: Volume fractions of the phases in a 90 wt% Zn brass
questions.body_md:
Determine the relative amounts (in terms of volume fractions) of the phases for 90 wt% Zn-10 wt% Cu at $400\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Take the densities of Zn and Cu to be $6.83$ and $8.77\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ respectively.

![The copper-zinc phase diagram, temperature against wt% Zn](pack:l5-cu-zn)
questions.solution_md:
### What the diagram and the lever rule give

This is a Cu-Zn alloy at $400\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, where

$$C_\varepsilon = 87\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Zn}\qquadC_\eta = 97\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Zn}$$

$$W_\varepsilon = \frac{C_\eta - C_0}{C_\eta - C_\varepsilon} = \frac{97 - 90}{97 - 87} = 0.70\qquad W_\eta = 0.30$$

### Mass fractions are not volume fractions

To convert, each phase's own density is needed, and each is computed from its composition and the two elemental densities:

$$\rho_\varepsilon = \frac{100}{\frac{C_{\mathrm{Zn}(\varepsilon)}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Zn}}} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{Cu}(\varepsilon)}}{\rho_{\mathrm{Cu}}}} = \frac{100}{\frac{87}{6.83} + \frac{13}{8.77}} = 7.03\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

$$\rho_\eta = \frac{100}{\frac{97}{6.83} + \frac{3}{8.77}} = 6.88\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

### Now the volume fractions

$$V_\varepsilon = \frac{\frac{W_\varepsilon}{\rho_\varepsilon}}{\frac{W_\varepsilon}{\rho_\varepsilon} + \frac{W_\eta}{\rho_\eta}} = \frac{\frac{0.70}{7.03}}{\frac{0.70}{7.03} + \frac{0.30}{6.88}} = 0.70$$

$$V_\eta = 0.30$$

The volume fractions come out almost equal to the mass fractions here, because the two phases are both nearly all zinc and so have nearly the same density. That is a coincidence of this alloy, not a rule: where two phases differ in density the two sets of fractions part company.

questions.title: Are these magnesium-lead measurements even possible?
questions.body_md:
A colleague engineer is running quality control at a casting facility, and he is seeing some odd measurements from their magnesium-lead batch. The furnace is running at $460\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and he just tested a $6.70\ \mathrm{kg}$ sample. His measurements show $4.23\ \mathrm{kg}$ of primary alpha phase (formed during initial cooling) and $6.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of total alpha phase (including what formed later). Something feels off about these numbers.

Before he calls for equipment recalibration or halts production, he is asking if you can check whether it is even physically possible to have these measurements in a $6.70\ \mathrm{kg}$ sample at $460\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. If not, what's wrong with these numbers?

![The magnesium-lead phase diagram, temperature against wt% Pb](pack:l5-mg-pb)
questions.solution_md:
### Convert the masses to mass fractions

$$W_{\alpha'} = \frac{4.23}{6.70} = 0.6313\qquadW_\alpha = \frac{6.00}{6.70} = 0.8955$$

### Read the compositions off the diagram

At $460\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $C_\alpha = 41\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$, $C_{\mathrm{Mg_2Pb}} = 81\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$, and $C_{\mathrm{eutectic}} = 66\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$.

### The lever rule for primary alpha

$$W_{\alpha'} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{eutectic}} - C_0}{C_{\mathrm{eutectic}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{66 - C_0}{66 - 41} = 0.6313$$

Solving gives $C_0 = 50.2\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$.

### The lever rule for total alpha

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_{\mathrm{Mg_2Pb}} - C_0}{C_{\mathrm{Mg_2Pb}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{81 - C_0}{81 - 41} = 0.8955$$

And this value of $C_0$ is $45.2\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Pb}$.

### The verdict

A sample has one composition. These two measurements imply two different ones, so the alloy is not possible and the measurements are inconsistent with each other rather than merely imprecise.

questions.title: Composition from primary and total alpha fractions
questions.body_md: Consider the hypothetical eutectic phase diagram for metals A and B, which is similar to that for the lead-tin system. Assume that (1) $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases exist at the A and B extremes of the phase diagram, respectively; (2) the eutectic composition is 47 wt% B-53 wt% A; and (3) the composition of the $\beta$ phase at the eutectic temperature is 92.6 wt% B-7.4 wt% A. Determine the composition of an alloy that will yield primary $\alpha$ and total $\alpha$ mass fractions of 0.356 and 0.693, respectively.
questions.solution_md:
### Two lever rules, two unknowns

Primary $\alpha$ is what forms before the eutectic reaction, so its lever arm runs to the eutectic composition. Total $\alpha$ includes the $\alpha$ inside the eutectic structure, so its lever arm runs to the $\beta$ composition. The unknowns are the alloy composition $C_0$ and the $\alpha$ composition $C_\alpha$.

### Primary alpha

$$W_{\alpha'} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{eutectic}} - C_0}{C_{\mathrm{eutectic}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{47 - C_0}{47 - C_\alpha} = 0.356$$

### Total alpha

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{92.6 - C_0}{92.6 - C_\alpha} = 0.693$$

### Solve the pair

Rearranging each for $C_0$ and eliminating it gives $C_\alpha$, and substituting back gives the alloy composition:

$$C_0 = 32.6\ \mathrm{wt\%\ B}$$

questions.title: What happens to a 30 wt% Sn solder at the eutectic temperature
questions.body_md:
As a quality engineer at a solder manufacturing plant, you're developing a new lead-tin solder. You've created a mixture that's 70 wt% Pb-30 wt% Sn and heated it to exactly the eutectic temperature. Your supervisor asks:

- **(a)** What phases are present at this moment?
- **(b)** If you lower the temperature by just $1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, what phases will form?
- **(c)** What makes this composition special at this exact temperature?

![The lead-tin phase diagram, with the 183 degree C eutectic isotherm at 61.9 wt% Sn](pack:l5-pb-sn)
questions.solution_md:
### Where the alloy sits

The eutectic composition is 61.9 wt% Sn and the eutectic temperature is $183\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. At 30 wt% Sn this alloy is hypoeutectic: it lies to the left of the eutectic point.

### (a) At exactly the eutectic temperature

The vertical line at 30 wt% Sn meets the eutectic isotherm inside the $\alpha + L$ field, so $\alpha$ and liquid are both present. The tie line along the isotherm gives their compositions as the two ends of that line:

$$C_\alpha = 18.3\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}\qquadC_L = 61.9\ \mathrm{wt\%\ Sn}$$

### (b) One degree lower

Below the isotherm no liquid can exist. The remaining liquid, which is sitting at exactly the eutectic composition, undergoes the eutectic reaction

$$L \rightarrow \alpha + \beta$$

so the alloy becomes the proeutectoid $\alpha$ that had already formed plus eutectic structure, and the phases present are $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

### (c) Why this temperature is special

$183\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is the eutectic isotherm: the lowest temperature at which any liquid can exist in the lead-tin system, and the only temperature at which three phases ($\alpha$, $\beta$ and $L$) coexist in equilibrium. Liquid does not freeze over a range here, it transforms at a single temperature, which is exactly the property that makes eutectic compositions useful as solders.

questions.title: Ferrite, cementite and pearlite from 1.15 wt% C austenite
questions.body_md:
Consider $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of austenite containing 1.15 wt% C, cooled to below $727\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

- **(a)** What is the proeutectoid phase?
- **(b)** How many kilograms each of total ferrite and cementite form?
- **(c)** How many kilograms each of pearlite and the proeutectoid phase form?
questions.solution_md:
### (a) Which side of the eutectoid

The proeutectoid phase will be $\mathrm{Fe_3C}$, since 1.15 wt% C is greater than the eutectoid composition of 0.76 wt% C. The alloy is hypereutectoid.

### (b) Total ferrite

$$W_\alpha = \frac{6.70 - C_0}{6.70 - 0.022} = \frac{6.70 - 1.15}{6.678} = 0.83$$

Multiplied by the total mass of $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, this gives $0.83\ \mathrm{kg}$ of total ferrite.

### Total cementite

$$W_{\mathrm{Fe_3C}} = \frac{C_0 - 0.022}{6.70 - 0.022} = \frac{1.15 - 0.022}{6.678} = 0.17$$

so $0.17\ \mathrm{kg}$ of total cementite forms.

### (c) Pearlite

For pearlite the lever arm runs to the eutectoid composition rather than to pure ferrite:

$$W_p = \frac{6.70 - C_0}{6.70 - 0.76} = \frac{6.70 - 1.15}{5.94} = 0.93$$

which corresponds to a mass of $0.93\ \mathrm{kg}$.

### And the proeutectoid cementite

$$W_{\mathrm{Fe_3C}'} = \frac{C_0 - 0.76}{6.70 - 0.76} = \frac{1.15 - 0.76}{5.94} = 0.07$$

which is equivalent to $0.07\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the total $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass.

Note that (b) and (c) are different decompositions of the same kilogram: (b) counts the phases, (c) counts the microconstituents.

questions.title: Composition from primary and total beta fractions
questions.body_md: Consider a hypothetical eutectic phase diagram for metals A and B similar to the lead-tin system. Assume that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases exist at extremities of the phase diagram for A and B respectively; that the eutectic composition is 36 wt% A and 64 wt% B; and that the composition of the $\alpha$ phase at the eutectic temperature is 88 wt% A and 12 wt% B. Determine the composition of an alloy that will yield primary $\beta$ and total $\beta$ mass fractions of 0.367 and 0.768 respectively.
questions.solution_md:
### What is known

$$W_\beta = 0.768\qquad W_{\beta'} = 0.367$$

$$C_{\mathrm{eutectic}} = 64\ \mathrm{wt\%\ B}\qquadC_\alpha = 12\ \mathrm{wt\%\ B}$$

### Total beta

$$W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{C_0 - 12}{C_\beta - 12} = 0.768$$

### Primary beta

$$W_{\beta'} = \frac{C_0 - C_{\mathrm{eutectic}}}{C_\beta - C_{\mathrm{eutectic}}} = \frac{C_0 - 64}{C_\beta - 64} = 0.367$$

### Two equations and two unknowns

$$C_0 - 12 = 0.768\,C_\beta - 9.216$$

$$C_0 - 64 = 0.367\,C_\beta - 23.49$$

### Solving for the two compositions

$$C_0 = 75\ \mathrm{wt\%\ B}\qquadC_\beta = 94\ \mathrm{wt\%\ B}$$

questions.title: Proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite in a 0.35 wt% C steel
questions.body_md: Compute the mass fractions of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite that form in an iron-carbon alloy containing 0.35 wt% C.
questions.solution_md:
### Which side of the eutectoid

0.35 wt% C is below the eutectoid composition of 0.76 wt% C, so the alloy is hypoeutectoid and the proeutectoid phase is ferrite.

### Mass fraction of pearlite

$$W_p = \frac{T}{U + T} = \frac{C_0 - 0.022}{0.76 - 0.022} = \frac{0.35 - 0.022}{0.74} = 0.44$$

### Mass fraction of proeutectoid ferrite

$$W_{\alpha'} = \frac{U}{U + T} = \frac{0.76 - C_0}{0.76 - 0.022} = \frac{0.76 - 0.35}{0.74} = 0.56$$

The two sum to one, which is the check worth making: every gram of this steel is either proeutectoid ferrite or pearlite.

questions.title: Can a eutectoid ferrite fraction fix the composition?
questions.body_md: The mass fraction of eutectoid ferrite in an iron-carbon alloy is 0.71. On the basis of this information, is it possible to determine the composition of the alloy? If so, what is its composition? If this is not possible, explain why.
questions.solution_md:
### Why there are two cases

Eutectoid ferrite is the ferrite inside the pearlite, and it is found both in the hypoeutectoid region and in the hypereutectoid region. So the single number 0.71 does not by itself say which side of the eutectoid the alloy sits on, and both must be tested.

### Hypoeutectoid case

Here eutectoid ferrite is the total ferrite minus the proeutectoid ferrite:

$$W_{\alpha(\mathrm{eutectoid})} = W_\alpha - W_{\alpha'} = \frac{6.7 - C_0}{6.7 - 0.022} - \frac{0.76 - C_0}{0.76 - 0.022} = 0.71$$

Solving for $C_0$ gives $C_0 = 0.61\ \mathrm{wt\%\ C}$.

### Hypereutectoid case

Here there is no proeutectoid ferrite at all, so all the ferrite is in the pearlite and the eutectoid ferrite is the total ferrite:

$$W_{\alpha(\mathrm{eutectoid})} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{Fe_3C}} - C_0}{C_{\mathrm{Fe_3C}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{6.7 - C_0}{6.7 - 0.022} = 0.71$$

$$C_0 = 1.96\ \mathrm{wt\%\ C}$$

### The answer

Both are consistent with the information given, so the composition cannot be determined uniquely: it is either $0.61\ \mathrm{wt\%\ C}$ or $1.96\ \mathrm{wt\%\ C}$, and one further fact (the presence or absence of proeutectoid cementite, say) would settle it.
